aries.origin: Phrixus and Helle, children of King Athamas of Thessaly, had a hard time under their stepmother. Taking pity on them, Hermes sent a golden-fleeced ram to carry the two children through the sky. While flying, Helle fell into the sea, which was later called the Hellespont, meaning 'Helle's Sea' (today's Dardanelles). Phrixus reached Colchis, east of the Black Sea, safely, and Zeus honored the ram's service by placing it among the stars. The oldest record is the Babylonian MUL.APIN, which calls it 'the Hired Man.' In Egypt it was linked to the sun god Amun-Ra, who announced the spring equinox.
aries.tip: Its stars are faint, so in cities you may see only Hamal and Sheratan. Look just west of Taurus.

stars.mesarthim: A binary system of two similarly bright stars 7.8 arcseconds apart. The origin of the name is uncertain; the IAU approved it in 2016 as the official name of γ² Arietis.
stars.sheratan: The name means 'the two signs' in Arabic, because this star and Gamma Arietis once marked the northern hemisphere's spring equinox point.
stars.hamal: The name comes from the Arabic 'Ras al-Hamal,' meaning 'head of the ram.' In Arabic tradition, Aries was simply called 'the sheep.'
stars.botein: The name comes from 'Al Buteyn,' a diminutive of the Arabic 'al-baṭn,' meaning 'the belly.' The IAU approved it as the official name in 2016.
stars.bharani: 'Bharani' is the name of the second nakshatra (lunar mansion) in Hindu astronomy.

taurus.origin: Zeus, who was famously unfaithful, fell for Europa, a Phoenician princess playing by the seashore. He turned into a dazzling white bull and mingled with the king's herd; when Europa playfully climbed on his back, he plunged into the sea and swam all the way to Crete with her. In Greece there is also a story that Zeus turned his lover Io into a heifer to hide her from Hera, and Acusilaus linked this bull to the Cretan Bull that Heracles captured. In older Mesopotamia it connects to the 'Bull of Heaven' from the Epic of Gilgamesh. In the sky, only the front half of the bull is often drawn.
taurus.tip: It's easy once you find the red first-magnitude star Aldebaran and the small star cluster known as the Pleiades.

stars.tianguan: The name comes from the Chinese 'Tianguan' (天關), meaning 'Gate of Heaven,' a star within the Chinese asterism Bi (畢宿). It is an eclipsing binary whose stars cover each other about every 133 days.
stars.aldebaran: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Dabarān,' meaning 'the follower,' because it rises after the Pleiades cluster. Its brightness varies slightly between magnitude 0.75 and 0.95.
stars.chamukuy: 'Chamukuy' means 'little bird' in Yucatec Maya. The IAU approved it as the official name in 2017. It is a Delta Scuti–type variable whose brightness changes very slightly.
stars.prima-hyadum: The name is Latin for 'first of the Hyades.' It belongs to the Hyades cluster that forms the bull's face.
stars.elnath: The name means 'the one butting with horns' in Arabic. It marks the tip of the bull's horn.
stars.bibing: Every 3.95 days the two stars eclipse each other, changing its brightness between magnitude 3.37 and 3.91. The name comes from 'the handle of the net' in the Chinese asterism Bi (畢宿).
stars.secunda-hyadum: The name is Latin for 'second of the Hyades.' The IAU approved it as the official name in 2017.
stars.ain: The name means 'the eye' in Arabic. It is an orange giant belonging to the Hyades cluster.

gemini.origin: Leda, queen of Sparta, was said to have borne twin brothers by Zeus, who had taken the form of a swan, and her husband Tyndareus. Pollux, a son of Zeus, was immortal, while Castor was the son of a mortal. Castor was skilled at horsemanship, and Pollux at boxing and arms; the two were always together. When Castor died, Pollux was overcome with grief and begged Zeus to let him die too; moved by their brotherly love, Zeus turned them both into stars. The Greeks regarded the twins as protectors of sailors. In Babylon these two stars were called 'the Great Twins.'
gemini.tip: The two bright stars Castor and Pollux stand side by side, which makes them easy to find. Look to the upper left of Orion.

stars.pollux: Named after Pollux, the immortal twin of myth. It is actually brighter than Castor and is the leading star of Gemini.
stars.wasat: The name means 'the middle' in Arabic. It is a binary system in which an orange companion orbits a yellow-white primary.
stars.mekbuda: A yellow supergiant that swells and shrinks over about 10.2 days, varying between magnitude 3.7 and 4.2. The name means 'the folded paw of the lion' in Arabic.
stars.alhena: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Han'a,' meaning 'the brand on the camel's neck.' It shines at Pollux's foot.
stars.castor: Named after Castor, the mortal twin of myth. It is a multiple star system in which several stars orbit one another.
stars.mebsuta: The name means 'the outstretched paw' in Arabic. It comes from the paw of a giant lion that ancient Arabs drew across several constellations.
stars.tejat: A red giant that varies between magnitude 2.75 and 3.02. The name comes from the old South Arabian word 'Tihyat,' whose meaning is unknown.
stars.propus: A red giant that varies between magnitude 3.1 and 3.7. The name means 'forefoot' in Greek.
stars.lambda: Lambda (λ) of Gemini. It has no proper name.

cancer.origin: For his second labor, Heracles had to defeat the monstrous water serpent, the Hydra. Hera, who hated Heracles, sent a giant crab to help the serpent; the crab bit Heracles on the toe but was crushed underfoot. To reward the crab that died fighting for her, Hera is said to have raised its image into the sky as a constellation. In the 2nd century Ptolemy called it 'Karkinos' (the crab). The Greeks and Romans saw the central Praesepe (the Beehive Cluster) as a manger from which two donkeys feed, and in Babylon it was called 'Alulu' (MUL.AL.LUL).
cancer.tip: It is made of faint stars and is barely visible in cities. Look under a dark sky between Leo and Gemini.

stars.asellus-australis: The name is Latin for 'southern donkey colt.' It comes from the idea that Praesepe (the Beehive Cluster) is a manger, with the two stars on either side being the donkeys.
stars.asellus-borealis: The name is Latin for 'northern donkey.' It shines just north of Praesepe.
stars.yuyu: 'Yuyu' means freshwater crab in Javanese, and it is also the Balinese name for Cancer. It is a multiple star system in which several stars orbit one another.
stars.tarf: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Ṭarf,' meaning 'the end' or 'the edge.' The IAU approved it as the official name in 2018.
stars.acubens: The name means 'the claw' in Arabic. It is a multiple system made of four stars.

leo.origin: In an age of turmoil, when comets often appeared, a meteor that fell from the Moon is said to have turned into a golden lion and landed in the Nemean valley. This lion was far bigger and fiercer than an ordinary lion and tormented people. For his first labor, Heracles had to catch it; when bow, spear and club all failed, he wrestled it bare-handed and won. Zeus honored his son's courage by raising the lion to the sky, and Ovid called this constellation 'the lion of Heracles.' In Babylon it was called 'the Great Lion' (UR.GU.LA), and Regulus was regarded as 'the King's Star.'
leo.tip: It's easy once you spot the backward-question-mark shape of the mane, which begins at the first-magnitude star Regulus.

stars.regulus: The name is Latin for 'little king.' In Babylon it was called 'the King's Star,' standing at the lion's chest. It spins so fast that it bulges at the equator.
stars.eta: A star in the Arabic asterism 'al-Jabhah,' meaning 'the forehead of the lion.' It has no proper name.
stars.algieba: The name means 'the forehead' in Arabic. Through a telescope it splits into two stars, making it a binary.
stars.adhafera: The name means 'the lock of hair' in Arabic. It originally referred to Coma Berenices and was mistakenly attached to this star in the 17th century.
stars.rasalas: The name is short for 'Ras al-Asad al-Shamaliyy,' meaning 'the northern part of the lion's head.'
stars.algenubi: The name means 'the southern star of the lion's head' in Arabic. It sits at the end of the 'sickle' that outlines the lion's head.
stars.zosma: The name means 'girdle' in Ancient Greek, and it sits where the lion's hindquarters would be.
stars.chertan: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Kharatān,' meaning 'the two small ribs.' It originally referred to the stars δ and θ together.
stars.denebola: The name comes from the Arabic 'Dhanab al-Asad,' meaning 'the lion's tail.' It is relatively close to Earth, so it looks bright.

virgo.origin: Virgo is said to depict Astraea, goddess of justice. Even after the gods left the earth, she stayed among humans and taught justice, but when people sank into lies and violence she finally returned to the heavens. In old star pictures she holds an ear of wheat, so she was also read as Demeter, goddess of grain, or as her daughter Persephone returning from the underworld. Hyginus linked this constellation to Erigone, daughter of Icarius. The oldest Babylonian records call it 'the Furrow' of the goddess Shala, who holds an ear of grain.
virgo.tip: Follow the Great Spring Arc from Arcturus to Spica to find it. Spica is the brightest star.

stars.spica: The name is Latin for 'the maiden's ear of wheat.' It shines blue at the tip of the ear the maiden holds. It is a close binary, so its brightness varies slightly.
stars.porrima: Named after Porrima (Antevorta), the Roman goddess of prophecy. It is a binary in which two similar stars orbit each other.
stars.zaniah: The name means 'the corner' in Arabic.
stars.zavijava: The name means something like 'the corner of the barking dog' in Arabic. A star of a type similar to the Sun is nearby.
stars.minelauva: Its brightness varies slightly between magnitude 3.32 and 3.40. The name comes from the Arabic 'in the lunar mansion al-Awwa,' and the IAU approved it as the official name in 2017.
stars.vindemiatrix: The name is Latin for 'the grape-gatherer' (a woman who picks grapes).
stars.syrma: The name means 'the train of a robe' in Ancient Greek.
stars.heze: The name first appeared in the 1951 star atlas 'Atlas Coeli,' and where it came from is unknown. The IAU approved it as the official name in 2018.

libra.origin: Libra is said to be the scales carried by Astraea, goddess of justice. She weighed people's good and evil to decide their fates, and was placed in the sky in honor of her work for justice and fairness. In fact, for a long time this constellation was seen as the claws of the Scorpion. Aratus called these stars 'the claws,' and the Arabic 'Zubana' also means 'the scorpion's claws.' In Babylon it was called 'Zibanu,' the scales of the sun god Shamash. In Roman times it became its own scales constellation next to Virgo.
libra.tip: Its stars are mostly faint, so a dark spot with an open southern view is best. Look to the lower right of Spica in Virgo.

stars.zubenelgenubi: The name means 'the southern claw' in Arabic. Through binoculars it splits into two stars.
stars.zubeneschamali: The name means 'the northern claw' in Arabic. It is the brightest star in Libra.
stars.zubenelhakrabi: The name comes from the Arabic 'Zuban al-ʿAqrab,' meaning 'the scorpion's claw.'
stars.delta: An eclipsing binary whose two stars cover each other about every 2 days 8 hours, changing its brightness between magnitude 4.9 and 5.9.
stars.brachium: The name is Latin for 'arm.' It was once Gamma Scorpii, until Benjamin Gould moved it to Libra as Sigma Librae in 1851.
stars.iota: A complex multiple star system in which several stars orbit one another. The primary is blue-white and part of a binary with a 23-year period.

scorpio.origin: Orion, the giant hunter, boasted that he was the strongest in the world and could hunt any beast. Angered by this arrogance, Hera is said to have sent a scorpion to destroy him. The god who sent it differs by tradition: Hesiod, Hyginus and Ovid say it was Gaia, goddess of the earth, while Aratus says it was Artemis. For this deed the scorpion became a constellation. That's why, when Scorpius rises, Orion flees and sets in the west, and the two constellations are never seen in the sky together.
scorpio.tip: The red first-magnitude star Antares is your guide. Since it sits low, look from a place with an open southern horizon, such as by the sea or on wide flat ground.

stars.antares: The name means 'rival of Ares (Mars)' in Ancient Greek, because its red color resembles Mars. It glows red at the scorpion's heart and is a variable star whose brightness changes slightly.
stars.acrab: Acrab means 'scorpion' in Arabic. It is also known by its Greek name Graffias ('the crab'). It is a multiple star system made of several stars, so it splits apart in a telescope.
stars.dschubba: The name means 'the scorpion's forehead' in Arabic. It suddenly brightened in 2000 and still varies in brightness.
stars.alniyat: Alniyat means 'the arteries' in Arabic. It was a name for the two stars Sigma and Tau on either side of Antares (the scorpion's heart); Sigma lies north of Antares.
stars.pi: A star near the claws. It is a multiple star system in which two or more stars orbit one another.
stars.tau: A star south of Antares that, together with Sigma, flanks Antares. Its Hawaiian name Paikauhale means 'the wanderer who roams from house to house.'
stars.epsilon: Among the bright stars of Scorpius, it is one of the closest to Earth. Its name means 'clearly seen' in the language of the Wardaman, an Aboriginal Australian people.
stars.mu: A binary system at the start of the tail's curve. Its name means '(two) lions' eyes' in Khoekhoe.
stars.zeta2: Zeta¹, right beside it, is a blue-white supergiant about 6,000 light-years away. The two simply line up in the same direction and are unrelated.
stars.sargas: A bright star at the left end of the tail's curve. The name is said to come from Sumerian.
stars.girtab: A star where the tail curves upward. Girtab is said to mean 'scorpion' in Sumerian.
stars.shaula: The name means 'the raised (tail)' in Arabic. It shines at the tip of the scorpion's stinger and is the second brightest star in Scorpius after Antares.

sagittarius.origin: Centaurs are a race with the upper body of a human and the lower body of a horse. Most were wild, but Chiron alone was refined and wise; taught music, medicine, hunting and prophecy by Apollo and Artemis, he is said to have taught astronomy to Heracles and martial arts to Achilles. While Heracles was fighting centaurs, an arrow dipped in Hydra's poison accidentally struck Chiron's foot. Being immortal, he could not even die; after great suffering he gave his immortality to Prometheus and passed away, and Zeus placed him among the stars. Eratosthenes saw this archer as the satyr Crotus, inventor of archery. In Babylon it was called 'Pabilsaĝ.'
sagittarius.tip: Look for the Southern Dipper (the Milk Dipper), toward the center of the summer Milky Way. It sits low in the southern sky, so an open horizon helps.

stars.namalsadirah: The name comes from the Arabic for 'the returning ostriches.' It originally referred to four stars together, and φ was the first of them.
stars.kaus-borealis: The name combines the Arabic for 'bow' with the Latin for 'north.' It sits at the upper end of the bow the archer holds.
stars.nunki: The name comes from 'Nunki,' the Sumerian name for Eridu, the central city of Abzu, the sea of underground fresh water.
stars.ascella: The name means 'armpit' in Late Latin. It is a binary system with two stars of similar brightness close together.
stars.kaus-australis: The name combines the Arabic for 'bow' with the Latin for 'south.' It spins so fast that its temperature and size differ between pole and equator.
stars.alnasl: The name means 'the arrowhead' in Arabic. It sits at the tip of the teapot's spout.
stars.kaus-media: The name combines the Arabic for 'bow' with the Latin for 'middle.'
stars.hamalwarid: A red giant whose brightness hardly changes, staying between magnitude 3.08 and 3.12.

capricorn.origin: Pan, god of flocks, was happily celebrating at a feast of the gods on the banks of the Nile when the giant Typhon appeared and attacked the gods, who fled by turning into animals. Pan, rushing through his spell, got mixed up and ended up with the upper body of a goat and the lower body of a fish. When Zeus was in danger, Pan blew his reed pipe and drove Typhon away, and in gratitude Zeus made the 'sea-goat,' half goat and half fish, a constellation. Some stories link it to the goat Amalthea, who nursed Zeus with her milk. In Babylon it was called the 'goat-fish' (MUL.SUḪUR.MAŠ), the symbol of the water god Ea.
capricorn.tip: Its faint stars form a big inverted triangle. Look low in the southern sky, below the Summer Triangle.

stars.dabih: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Dhābiḥ,' meaning 'the slaughterer.' It is said to come from the custom of offering sacrifices when this star first rose before sunrise.
stars.psi: Psi (ψ) of Capricornus. In Chinese astronomy it is part of 'Tiantian' (天田), meaning 'the Heavenly Field.'
stars.omega: Omega (ω) of Capricornus. It has no proper name.
stars.yen: The name 'Yen' comes from the state of Yan (燕), one of the old states of China. It is a binary system with a white dwarf companion.
stars.deneb-algedi: The name means 'the goat's tail' in Arabic. It is an eclipsing variable whose brightness changes by about 0.2 magnitude over a 24.5-hour period.
stars.algedi: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Jady,' meaning 'the goat.' The IAU approved it as the official name of this star in 2016.

aquarius.origin: When Hebe, goddess of youth, sprained her ankle and could no longer pour wine for the gods, Zeus is said to have turned into an eagle and carried the Trojan boy Ganymede, who was tending sheep on Mount Ida, up to Olympus. Ganymede then took on the job of filling the gods' cups. The constellation shows Ganymede holding a jar overflowing with water. Other stories see him as Deucalion, who survived the Great Flood, or as Cecrops, the Athenian king who offered water instead of wine to the gods. In Babylon it was called 'the Great One' (GU.LA), a star of the water god Ea, and in Egypt it was tied to the flooding of the Nile.
aquarius.tip: Its stars are faint, so a place with little city light is best. Look in the southern sky below the Great Square of Autumn.

stars.albali: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Bāliʿ,' meaning 'the swallower.'
stars.sadalsuud: The name comes from the Arabic 'Saʿd al-Suʿūd,' meaning 'the luck of lucks.' It is one of the brightest stars in Aquarius.
stars.sadalmelik: The name comes from the Arabic 'Saʿd al-Malik,' meaning 'the luck of the king.' It is a supergiant about 690 light-years from Earth.
stars.sadachbia: The name means 'the luck of the tents (houses)' in Arabic. The IAU approved it as the official name in 2016.
stars.sadaltager: A binary system of two stars orbiting closely, with a combined magnitude of 3.65. Its old Arabic name was 'al-ʿAqr al-ʾAkbiyah.'
stars.ancha: The name means 'hip' in Medieval Latin.
stars.hydor: The name means 'water' in Greek. It is a red giant that varies between magnitude 3.57 and 3.80.
stars.skat: The name comes from the Arabic 'al-Sāq,' meaning 'the shin.'

pisces.origin: Aphrodite, goddess of beauty, and her son Eros were resting by the Euphrates when the monster Typhon appeared. Startled, the two gods turned into fish and leapt into the river to hide, and their forms are said to have risen into the sky as a constellation. The same story appears in Hyginus's 'Poetic Astronomy' and Ovid's 'Fasti,' and in the Roman version the two gods flee riding on the backs of two fish. The two fish are said to be tied with a cord, a detail believed to come from two Babylonian constellations, 'the Great Swallow' and 'Anunitum, the Lady of the Heavens.'
pisces.tip: It is made of faint stars. Look below the Great Square of Autumn and follow the V shape.

stars.alrescha: The name comes from the Arabic 'ar-Rishā,' meaning 'the cord.' It shines at the knot where the cord joining the two fish meets.
stars.revati: 'Revati' is the name of a nakshatra (lunar mansion) in Indian astronomy, meaning 'wealthy' in Sanskrit. It is a multiple star system in which several stars orbit together.
stars.omega: The name 'Pili' comes from the Chinese asterism 'Pili' (霹靂), meaning 'thunder.' Old Arabic catalogs called it 'the tail of the fish.'
stars.iota: A star of a type similar to the Sun, about 45 light-years from Earth. In China it is the fourth star of the 'Pili' asterism.
stars.theta: Theta (θ) of Pisces. It has no proper name.
stars.gamma: The brightest of the stars making up the western fish. In 2021 an exoplanet was discovered around it.
stars.kuton: In Chinese astronomy it is part of 'Waiping' (外屏), meaning 'the outer screen.'
stars.torcular: The name comes from the old name 'Torcularis Septentrionalis' (the northern wine press), and the IAU approved it as the official name in 2017.
stars.alpherg: The name is said to come from the Arabic 'al-Farġ,' meaning 'the emptying.' The IAU approved it as the official name in 2018.
stars.chi: A star in the northern fish. It has no proper name.
stars.phi: A star in the northern fish. It has no proper name.
stars.tau: A star in the northern fish. It has no proper name.

orion.origin: Orion was a tall, strong hunter, a son of Poseidon, god of the sea. He was close to Artemis, goddess of the hunt, and Apollo, who disapproved, devised a trick: he had Artemis shoot an arrow at a distant black dot on the sea, and that dot was Orion. Grieving, Artemis raised him to the sky as a constellation. Another story says Orion was killed by a scorpion's sting, which is why Orion seems to flee and set in the west when Scorpius rises. It is the most eye-catching constellation of the winter night sky, and the belt of three stars in a row serves as a guide.
orion.tip: The three stars in a row (the Belt) are your guide. Confirm with red Betelgeuse at the upper left and blue Rigel at the lower right.

stars.betelgeuse: The name is said to come from Arabic, but its exact meaning is uncertain. It is so large that, if placed where the Sun is, it would reach nearly to Jupiter's orbit. It is a variable star whose brightness changes slightly.
stars.bellatrix: The name is Latin for 'female warrior.' It is a blue-white star at Orion's left shoulder.
stars.meissa: A star forming Orion's head. Its name is said to mean 'the shining one' in Arabic.
stars.alnitak: A star at one end of Orion's Belt; its name means 'the girdle' in Arabic. The Horsehead Nebula and the Flame Nebula are nearby.
stars.alnilam: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'string of pearls.' It sits in the middle of the three Belt stars.
stars.mintaka: A star at one end of the Belt; its name means 'the belt' in Arabic. It lies almost exactly on the celestial equator, so it rises nearly due east and sets nearly due west.
stars.saiph: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the sword of the giant.' It marks Orion's knee.
stars.rigel: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'foot.' It marks Orion's left foot and, despite the name, is the brightest star in the constellation.

ursa-major.origin: Zeus loved the beautiful nymph Callisto, and when Hera found out, she jealously turned Callisto into a bear. Years later, Callisto's son Arcas went hunting and came upon his mother in bear form; just as he unknowingly was about to shoot her, Zeus lifted them both into the sky as Ursa Major and Ursa Minor. The seven stars forming the bear's back and tail are the Big Dipper. Extending the line through the two stars at the end of the Dipper's bowl about five times leads to Polaris, so it has long been used as a guide.
ursa-major.tip: Link the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl (Dubhe and Merak) and extend the line about five times to find Polaris.

stars.dubhe: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'bear.' Together with Merak it is a pointer for finding Polaris.
stars.merak: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'loin.' Connect it with Dubhe to find Polaris.
stars.phecda: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'thigh.' It sits at a lower corner of the Big Dipper's bowl.
stars.megrez: The name means 'the root of the tail' in Arabic. It is the faintest star of the Big Dipper.
stars.alioth: The name comes from Arabic. It is the brightest star in Ursa Major and is known as an unusual star with a strong magnetic field.
stars.mizar: The faint Alcor beside it was used long ago as an eyesight test. Through a telescope, Mizar is a multiple star system in which several stars orbit together.
stars.alkaid: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the leader of the group.' It is the star at the very end of the Big Dipper's handle.

ursa-minor.origin: Ursa Minor is the partner of Ursa Major and is said to be Callisto's son Arcas. Another story says it is the nymph who hid and raised the infant Zeus, raised to the sky. The star at the tip of its tail is Polaris, which always points north, making it a guide for sailors and travelers. Because it lies close to the celestial north pole, it never sets below the horizon in Korea all year round.
ursa-minor.tip: Polaris is the tip of the tail. Find Polaris first using the end of the Big Dipper's bowl or the W of Cassiopeia.

stars.polaris: It points almost exactly at the north celestial pole today, which is why it is called the North Star. Because Earth's rotation axis slowly shifts, other stars will take over as the pole star in time.
stars.yildun: The name comes from the Turkish word for 'star.' It forms part of the handle of the Little Dipper.
stars.epsilon-umi: A star forming the handle of Ursa Minor. It has no proper name.
stars.zeta-umi: A star at a corner of the Little Dipper's bowl. It has no proper name.
stars.eta-umi: A star at a corner of the Little Dipper's bowl. It has no proper name.
stars.pherkad: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'calf.' Together with Kochab, it was called 'the Guardians of the Pole.'
stars.kochab: Around 1500 BCE it was the star closest to the north pole. Together with Pherkad, it was called 'the Guardians of the Pole.'

cassiopeia.origin: Cassiopeia was queen of Ethiopia, and she boasted that her daughter Andromeda was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, the Nereids. An angry Poseidon sent a sea monster to ravage the kingdom, and as punishment Cassiopeia is said to have been lifted into the sky, still seated on her throne, to circle the north pole. In the sky she looks like a W or an M, so she is easy to find, and she serves as the guide opposite the Big Dipper when looking for Polaris.
cassiopeia.tip: Its W or M shape makes it easy to find. It lies on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper.

stars.caph: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'hand.' It is a variable star whose brightness changes only very slightly.
stars.shedar: The name means 'the breast' in Arabic. It marks the queen Cassiopeia's chest.
stars.navi: A star whose brightness varies widely; it once brightened to nearly first magnitude. 'Navi' is the astronaut Gus Grissom's middle name, Ivan, spelled backwards.
stars.ruchbah: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'knee.' It is an eclipsing binary whose two stars cover each other, so its brightness changes slightly.
stars.segin: A star forming Cassiopeia's chair. The origin of the name is uncertain.

cygnus.origin: It is said to come from the story of Zeus turning into a swan to visit Leda, queen of Sparta. Another story says it is Cycnus, a friend of Phaethon, who dove into the river to search for Phaethon after he fell while driving the sun god's chariot, and was turned into a swan and became a star. Because of its cross shape it is also called the Northern Cross, and it looks like a swan flying right through the middle of the Milky Way. Deneb forms the Summer Triangle together with Vega and Altair.
cygnus.tip: It flies over the Milky Way in the shape of a cross. Deneb is one corner of the Summer Triangle.

stars.deneb: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'tail.' Though it is very far away, it appears as a first-magnitude star because it is intrinsically tremendously bright.
stars.sadr: The name means 'the breast' in Arabic. It sits at the crossing point of the cross and is surrounded by a wide spread of nebulae.
stars.albireo: A famous double star: through a small telescope you can see an orange star and a blue star side by side. It marks the swan's beak.
stars.fawaris: A star at the swan's wing, and a multiple star system in which several stars orbit together.
stars.aljanah: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'wing.' It is an orange star forming the tip of one of the swan's wings.

lyra.origin: Lyra is said to be the lyre of Orpheus, the musician of Greek myth. Apollo gave Orpheus the instrument that Hermes had made from a tortoise shell, and with it Orpheus moved even birds and beasts. After he lost his wife Eurydice and later died, Zeus raised the lyre to the sky. Its brightest star, Vega, is known in East Asia as Zhinü, the Weaving Girl of the Qixi story, and is one corner of the Summer Triangle.
lyra.tip: The brightest star, Vega (the Weaving Girl star), is your guide. The small parallelogram below Vega is the body of the lyre.

stars.vega: The fifth brightest star in the night sky. The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the swooping eagle,' and in East Asia it is called the Weaving Girl star. In about 12,000 years it will become the North Star.
stars.zeta-lyr: A star forming a small triangle near Vega. It has no proper name.
stars.delta-lyr: A red giant forming one corner of the parallelogram below the lyre. Its brightness varies slightly.
stars.sulafat: The name means 'the tortoise' in Arabic. It connects to the story of Hermes making the lyre from a tortoise shell.
stars.sheliak: An eclipsing binary in which two stars orbit very closely and cover each other, changing its brightness. The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'tortoise.'

aquila.origin: Aquila is said to be the eagle that carried Zeus's thunderbolts. To bring the beautiful Trojan youth Ganymede to Olympus, Zeus either turned into an eagle or sent one, and Ganymede became the gods' wine-pouring attendant. This eagle is said to have risen to the sky as a constellation. Its brightest star, Altair, is known in East Asia as the Cowherd star, and it faces the Weaving Girl star Vega across the Milky Way.
aquila.tip: Find bright Altair (the Cowherd star) with a star on either side of it in a straight line.

stars.altair: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the flying eagle.' It spins so fast that it is flattened rather than round.
stars.tarazed: One of the three stars lined up right beside Altair. The name is said to come from the Persian word for 'the beam of a balance.'
stars.alshain: A star lined up with Altair and Tarazed. At about 45 light-years from Earth, it is relatively close.
stars.theta-aql: A star near the eagle's tail. It has no proper name.
stars.okab: A star at the tip of the eagle's wing. The name is said to come from the Arabic word for 'eagle.'
stars.almizan: A star about 50 light-years from Earth whose brightness changes only very slightly.
stars.lambda-aql: A star below the eagle's wing. It has no proper name.

canis-major.origin: Canis Major is said to be the faithful hunting dog that follows the hunter Orion. Another story says it is Laelaps, the dog that never lets its quarry escape, set in the sky by Zeus. Its brightest star, Sirius, is the brightest star in the night sky, and in ancient Egypt its rising just before dawn signaled the time of the Nile flood. Follow Orion's Belt downward to find Sirius.
canis-major.tip: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky. Follow Orion's Belt downward to reach it. It sits low, so a place with an open southern view helps.

stars.sirius: The name means 'the scorching one' in Greek. It looks brightest because it is both close and intrinsically bright, and it forms a pair with a small white companion, Sirius B.
stars.mirzam: The name means 'the announcer' in Arabic. It rises before Sirius, as though announcing its arrival.
stars.omicron2-cma: A bright blue supergiant far from us in Canis Major. It has no proper name.
stars.wezen: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'weight.' It is a supergiant of enormous size.
stars.aludra: The name is said to come from an Arabic word meaning 'the virgin.' It is a supergiant that looks bright despite being very far away.
stars.adhara: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'the virgins.' It is a bright star that emits a great deal of ultraviolet light.
stars.furud: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the short stars.' It sits at the big dog's forepaw.

pegasus.origin: Pegasus is said to be the winged horse born from the blood of Medusa when the hero Perseus cut off her head. The horse made a spring burst forth on Mount Helicon, and the hero Bellerophon tamed it and rode it to defeat the monster Chimera. Later it carried Zeus's thunderbolts on Olympus, and Zeus raised it to the sky as a constellation. You can find it by the Great Square of Autumn in the autumn night sky.
pegasus.tip: The Great Square of Autumn is your guide. One corner of the square is shared with Alpheratz in Andromeda.

stars.markab: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'ship' or 'vehicle.' It forms one corner of the Great Square of Autumn.
stars.scheat: The name is said to come from an Arabic word meaning 'shin.' It is a red giant whose brightness varies.
stars.alpheratz: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the horse's navel.' It now belongs to Andromeda but forms one corner of the Great Square of Autumn.
stars.algenib: A star forming one corner of the Great Square of Autumn. The name is said to come from an Arabic word meaning 'flank.'
stars.enif: The name means 'the nose' in Arabic. It is an orange supergiant at the tip of Pegasus's nose.
stars.homam: The name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the brave hero.' It sits at Pegasus's foreleg.
stars.biham: The name is said to come from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the young animals.' It sits near Pegasus's head.
stars.matar: The name means 'the rain' in Arabic. It is a star extending toward Pegasus's foreleg.

perseus.origin: Perseus was a hero, son of Zeus and Danaë. Knowing that looking into Medusa's eyes would turn him to stone, he is said to have cut off her head while watching her reflection in Athena's shield. On the way home he rescued Princess Andromeda, who was about to be offered to a sea monster, and married her. The star Algol means 'the demon's head' and corresponds to the hand of Perseus holding Medusa's head. Every year in mid-August the Perseid meteor shower pours down.
perseus.tip: Look below the W of Cassiopeia. Algol changes brightness about every 3 days. In mid-August you can also see the meteor shower.

stars.mirfak: The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'elbow.' Together with the young stars around it, it forms the Alpha Persei Moving Cluster.
stars.algol: An eclipsing binary whose brightness drops sharply about every 2.87 days. The name means 'the demon's head' in Arabic, and it is also called the eye of Medusa.
stars.atik: The name is said to come from a word meaning 'shoulder' in Arabic. It sits at Perseus's foot.
stars.epsilon-per: A star near Perseus's foot. It has no proper name.
stars.gamma-per: A star near the northern end of Perseus. It has no proper name.
stars.delta-per: A star forming the eastern part of Perseus's body. It has no proper name.
stars.miram: The name is said to come from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the one who contests.' Through a small telescope it is a double star.
stars.misam: A star at Perseus's arm. The name is said to come from the Arabic for 'wrist.'

cetus.origin: Cetus is the sea monster 'Ketos' of Greek myth that rose from the sea to devour Princess Andromeda. When Cassiopeia, queen of Ethiopia, boasted that her daughter was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, an angry Poseidon sent this monster to ravage the kingdom. The monster was eventually defeated by Perseus, and in the sky it appears stretched out near Andromeda and Perseus. Though it is named for a whale, old pictures draw it as more of a sea monster than a whale.
cetus.tip: It lies stretched across the southern sky in autumn and has few bright stars. Diphda (β) in the tail stands out most, so find that star first.

stars.diphda: The name comes from Arabic, and it is also called Deneb Kaitos. It sits in the whale's tail.
stars.menkar: The name means 'the nostrils' in Arabic. It marks the whale's nose.
stars.mira: The name is Latin for 'wonderful.' It was the first variable star whose changing brightness was recorded, in 1596, and it brightens and dims over a period of about 332 days.
stars.baten-kaitos: The name means 'the belly of the whale' in Arabic.
stars.eta-cet: An orange giant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 120 light-years from Earth.
stars.kaffaljidhma: A white star that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 80 light-years from Earth.
stars.tau-cet: A yellow star that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 12 light-years from Earth.
stars.iota-cet: An orange giant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 270 light-years from Earth.
stars.theta-cet: An orange giant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 110 light-years from Earth.
stars.delta-cet: A blue-white subgiant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 650 light-years from Earth.
stars.mu-cet: A yellow-white giant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 84 light-years from Earth.
stars.xi2-cet: A blue-white giant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 190 light-years from Earth.
stars.lambda-cet: A blue-white giant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 580 light-years from Earth.
stars.nu-cet: A yellow giant that forms part of the Cetus constellation lines. It is about 340 light-years from Earth.

puppis.origin: Puppis was originally part of Argo Navis, the constellation representing the giant ship Argo that the Greek hero Jason sailed. Argo Navis was so large that the 18th-century French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille split it into Carina, Vela and Puppis. Puppis is the part corresponding to the stern of the ship. It lies in the middle of the Milky Way, so it contains many star clusters.
puppis.tip: Look low in the southern sky in winter, below Sirius in Canis Major. It lies in the Milky Way, so on a clear night it looks full of stars through binoculars. A place with an open southern horizon is best.

stars.regor: The name is the Apollo astronaut Roger Chaffee's first name, Roger, read backwards. It is a binary system made of a very hot Wolf–Rayet star and a blue star.
stars.naos: The name means 'ship' in Greek. It is an O-type star among the hottest and brightest of all stars visible to the naked eye.
stars.ahadi: An orange supergiant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 810 light-years from Earth.
stars.tureis: A yellow-white bright giant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 64 light-years from Earth.
stars.nu-pup: A blue-white giant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 370 light-years from Earth.
stars.azmidi: A yellow supergiant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 1,200 light-years from Earth.
stars.hr2948: A blue-white subgiant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 350 light-years from Earth.
stars.3-pup: A white supergiant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines.
stars.11-pup: A yellow-white bright giant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 520 light-years from Earth.
stars.omicron-pup: A blue-white subgiant that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 1,420 light-years from Earth.
stars.hr2922: A blue-white star that forms part of the Puppis constellation lines. It is about 220 light-years from Earth.

antlia.origin: Antlia was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille while observing the southern sky. It is one of the constellations named to honor scientific instruments, and it represents the air pump used to create a vacuum. It is a relatively new constellation with no myth, and it has almost no bright stars, consisting only of a few faint ones.
antlia.tip: A faint constellation near the southern horizon in spring. It has no bright stars and is hard to find with the naked eye, so look in a dark place low in the sky below Hydra.

stars.alpha-ant: An orange giant that forms part of the Antlia constellation lines. It is about 370 light-years from Earth.
stars.epsilon-ant: An orange giant that forms part of the Antlia constellation lines. It is about 710 light-years from Earth.
stars.iota-ant: An orange giant that forms part of the Antlia constellation lines. It is about 190 light-years from Earth.

pavo.origin: Pavo was created by the Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius in the late 16th century, based on southern-sky observations by the navigators Keyser and de Houtman. It became widely known when it appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. It represents the peacock, the bird that symbolizes the goddess Hera in Greek myth.
pavo.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, use its leading star, Peacock, as your guide.

stars.peacock: The leading star of Pavo; its name is the English word for the bird.
stars.beta-pav: A white subgiant that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 140 light-years from Earth.
stars.delta-pav: A yellow subgiant that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 20 light-years from Earth.
stars.eta-pav: An orange giant that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 350 light-years from Earth.
stars.epsilon-pav: A white star that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 110 light-years from Earth.
stars.zeta-pav: An orange giant that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 220 light-years from Earth.
stars.gamma-pav: A yellow-white star that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 30 light-years from Earth.
stars.lambda-pav: A blue-white giant that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 1,430 light-years from Earth.
stars.pi-pav: A white star that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 130 light-years from Earth.
stars.xi-pav: A red giant that forms part of the Pavo constellation lines. It is about 470 light-years from Earth.

reticulum.origin: Reticulum was created by the French astronomer Lacaille in the 18th century. It represents the reticle, a grid of fine lines engraved in a telescope's eyepiece. Lacaille used this grid, which measures star positions, to observe the southern sky precisely. It has no myth and is made of a small diamond shape.
reticulum.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere you can find it as a small diamond shape.

stars.alpha-ret: A yellow giant that forms part of the Reticulum constellation lines. It is about 160 light-years from Earth.
stars.beta-ret: An orange subgiant that forms part of the Reticulum constellation lines. It is about 97 light-years from Earth.
stars.epsilon-ret: An orange subgiant that forms part of the Reticulum constellation lines. It is about 59 light-years from Earth.
stars.delta-ret: A red giant that forms part of the Reticulum constellation lines. It is about 530 light-years from Earth.

apus.origin: Apus was created in the late 16th century by the Dutch cartographer Plancius, based on observations by navigators. The bird of paradise is a bird native to the island of New Guinea. The name 'Apus' means 'without feet' in Greek, because in old Europe only the skins reached them without feet, so people believed the bird flew through the sky without feet. It lies close to the south celestial pole.
apus.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. Because it lies close to the south celestial pole, it can be seen all year round from most of the Southern Hemisphere.

camelopardalis.origin: Camelopardalis was created around 1612 by the Dutch astronomer Petrus Plancius. The giraffe has a long neck like a camel and spots like a leopard (pard), so in Latin it was called 'camelopardalis.' It has no myth and almost no bright stars, so even on a dark night its outline is hard to find. It stretches across the northern sky near Polaris.
camelopardalis.tip: A dim, faint constellation around Polaris. It has no distinct shape, so look in a place with little light pollution, between Cassiopeia and Ursa Major.

corvus.origin: Corvus is the white crow of Apollo, god of the sun, in Greek myth. Apollo sent it on an errand to fetch water in a cup, but the crow waited for figs to ripen and came back late. It lied that a water snake was to blame, was found out, and as punishment was turned into a black bird and placed in the sky. The neighboring Crater and Hydra also appear in this story.
corvus.tip: Look in the southern sky in spring, close to Spica in Virgo. The trapezoid made by four stars is your guide.

pyxis.origin: Pyxis was created by the French astronomer Lacaille in the 18th century and represents the mariner's compass used on ships. It lies close to Argo Navis, which once represented the great ship Argo, so in the past this area was seen as the ship's mast. It has no myth and is made of a few faint stars.
pyxis.tip: A faint constellation low in the southern sky in spring. It has no bright stars and is hard to find with the naked eye, so you need a dark sky and an open southern view.

volans.origin: Volans was created in the late 16th century by the Dutch cartographer Plancius and represents the flying fish leaping out of the water. People sailing the southern seas often saw flying fish, and this brings them into the sky. It became known when it appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603.
volans.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, look for a small constellation in the southern sky near Carina.

crux.origin: Crux is the symbol of the Southern Hemisphere sky, a small constellation in the shape of a cross. It was once seen as part of Centaurus, and became widely known in the Age of Discovery when European navigators used it to find direction in the southern seas. In 1679 the Frenchman Augustin Royer separated it as its own constellation. It is the smallest of the 88 constellations, and it appears on the flags of several countries, including Australia and New Zealand.
crux.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, extending the cross's long axis about 4.5 times leads to the direction of south, so it serves as a guide.

stars.acrux: The name combines alpha (α) and Crux. To the naked eye it looks like one star, but through a telescope it splits into a double star.
stars.gacrux: The name combines gamma (γ) and Crux. It is one of the closest M-type red giants to Earth.

piscis-austrinus.origin: Piscis Austrinus is the fish that drinks the water poured by Aquarius. It has been known since ancient times, and in myth it is sometimes said to be the parent of the two fish of Pisces. Fomalhaut, the brightest star in the autumn southern sky, sits where this fish's mouth would be.
piscis-austrinus.tip: Fomalhaut, a first-magnitude star shining alone low in the autumn southern sky, is your guide. There are no bright stars around it, so it stands out, but since it is low, a place with an open southern view is best.

triangulum-australe.origin: Triangulum Australe was created in the late 16th century from observations by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. It was given the name 'Southern' to distinguish it from Triangulum in the northern sky. Three bright stars form a large triangle, so it is easy to find in the Southern Hemisphere.
triangulum-australe.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, look for the large triangle made by three bright stars.

corona-australis.origin: Corona Australis is a small crown (a laurel wreath) lying beneath the feet of Sagittarius. It was already among the 48 constellations catalogued by the ancient Greek astronomer Ptolemy. Several stories are told about this crown. Its stars form a semicircle, so it is easy to recognize.
corona-australis.tip: In summer, look low in the southern sky, below Sagittarius. The semicircle shape of the stars is your guide. It is low, so you need an open southern horizon.

lacerta.origin: Lacerta was created in the 17th century by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius. He connected the faint stars between Andromeda and Cygnus into the shape of a lizard crawling in a zigzag. It has no myth and few bright stars. It lies near the Milky Way, so there are many stars around it.
lacerta.tip: In autumn, look near overhead between Cassiopeia and Cygnus for faint stars joined in a zigzag. A clear, dark night is best.

delphinus.origin: Delphinus is the dolphin that helped Poseidon, god of the sea, in Greek myth. When Poseidon proposed to the sea nymph Amphitrite and she fled and hid, the dolphin found her and persuaded her to marry him, and for this service it is said to have become a constellation in the sky. It is a neat little shape with a small diamond-shaped body and a tail star.
delphinus.tip: On summer nights, look for a small diamond near Altair in Aquila. A tail star extends below the diamond, so it looks like a dolphin.

vela.origin: Vela was originally part of Argo Navis, the constellation representing the great ship Argo that the Greek hero Jason sailed. When the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille divided Argo Navis, he set the ship's sails apart as Vela. It lies in the Milky Way, and its star Gamma² is a very hot Wolf–Rayet star.
vela.tip: From Korea it hangs only low, just above the southern horizon in spring, so it is hard to observe. Try on a clear night from a place with a completely open southern view.

grus.origin: Grus was created by Plancius in the late 16th century, based on the observations of Dutch navigators, and appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. It represents the crane, a bird with a long neck and legs. In the autumn southern sky it looks like a bird stretching its long neck below Piscis Austrinus.
grus.tip: Look low near the southern horizon in autumn, below Piscis Austrinus. Its leading star, Alnair, is the guide, but it is low in the sky, so you need an open southern view.

auriga.origin: Auriga shows a man driving a chariot pulled by horses. In Greek myth, one story says he is Erichthonius, the king of Athens who first made the chariot. The charioteer is said to carry the goat Capella on his shoulder and the kids (the Haedi) in his arm. The big pentagon shape in the winter night sky is easy to notice.
auriga.tip: In winter, find yellow first-magnitude Capella first, near overhead. The big pentagon formed by Capella and the other stars is Auriga.

telescopium.origin: Telescopium was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille and represents the telescope used to observe the heavens. It is one of the 14 constellations Lacaille newly defined in the southern sky, named after scientific instruments. It has no myth and is made of a few faint stars.
telescopium.tip: From Korea it barely hangs just above the southern horizon, so it is very hard to observe. Try on a summer night from a place with a completely open southern view.

coma-berenices.origin: Coma Berenices comes from the story of Berenice II, queen of Egypt. While her husband Ptolemy III was away at war, she offered her beautiful hair at a temple, praying for his safe return. When the hair disappeared, the court astronomer Conon is said to have explained that it had become stars in the sky. In the 16th century, Tycho Brahe and others treated it as its own constellation. The scattered cluster of stars looks like hair blowing in the wind.
coma-berenices.tip: In spring, between Denebola in Leo and Arcturus in Boötes, look for a hazy cluster of stars that looks like hair blowing loose. In a dark sky it is visible even to the naked eye.

stars.gamma-com: An orange giant that forms part of the Coma Berenices constellation lines. It is about 170 light-years from Earth.

bootes.origin: Boötes shows a man chasing the bear (Ursa Major), or a farmer driving oxen. Its leading star, Arcturus, means 'guardian of the bear' in Greek. In Greek myth, one story says he is Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto, and another says he is Icarius, who spread the cultivation of grapes. Following the handle of the Big Dipper leads you to Arcturus.
bootes.tip: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle and you reach the orange first-magnitude star Arcturus. The kite shape ending at Arcturus is Boötes.

hydrus.origin: Hydrus was created by Plancius in the late 16th century, based on the observations of Dutch navigators. Unlike the similarly named Hydra, it represents a small water snake in the southern sky. It lies close to the south celestial pole, so in the Southern Hemisphere its winding shape is easy to see.
hydrus.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. It lies close to the south celestial pole, so you can find it in the Southern Hemisphere.

hydra.origin: Hydra takes up the largest area of the sky of all 88 constellations. It represents the many-headed monster Hydra that Heracles defeated as one of his twelve labors in Greek myth. In the sky it begins below Cancer and stretches out long, carrying Corvus and Crater on its back.
hydra.tip: It stretches very long across the southern sky in spring. Southwest of Regulus in Leo, find the orange Alphard, which has no bright stars around it, and use it as your guide.

scutum.origin: Scutum was created in 1684 by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius to honor the victory of the Polish king John III Sobieski. The king is famous for defeating the Ottoman army at the Battle of Vienna in 1683. Its original name was 'Sobieski's Shield.' It is among the smaller of the 88 constellations and lies in the middle of the Milky Way.

serpens.origin: Serpens is the snake held in both hands by Ophiuchus. It is the only one of the 88 constellations split into two parts, a head and a tail. The two parts lie apart with Ophiuchus between them but are seen as a single snake. Ophiuchus is Asclepius, god of medicine, and the snake symbolizes healing.
serpens.tip: The head lies to the right (west) of Ophiuchus and the tail to the left (east). Find Ophiuchus first in the southern sky in summer, and you can find the snake on both sides.

ophiuchus.origin: Ophiuchus shows Asclepius, god of medicine, holding a snake in both hands. Asclepius was so skilled a physician that he could even bring the dead back to life; Zeus, who disapproved, struck him down with a thunderbolt, and a grieving Apollo is said to have raised him to the sky. The Sun passes through it from late November to mid-December, so it is also called the '13th zodiac constellation.'
ophiuchus.tip: In summer, look in the southern sky for a big pentagon (house shape) above Scorpius. It lies between Hercules and Scorpius, and Serpens wraps around it on both sides.

phoenix.origin: Phoenix was created by the Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius in the late 16th century, based on southern-sky observations by the navigators Keyser and de Houtman. It became known when it appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. It represents the phoenix, the legendary bird that burns itself to ashes when its time comes to die and is reborn. It depicts the Western phoenix, but in Korean it is called the 'Bonghwang' constellation.
phoenix.tip: From Korea it hangs only very low above the southern horizon, so it is hard to observe. In late autumn, from a place with a completely open southern view, try to find its leading star, Ankaa.

corona-borealis.origin: Corona Borealis is the crown of Ariadne, princess of Crete, in Greek myth. Ariadne helped the hero Theseus defeat the Minotaur in the labyrinth but was left alone on the island of Naxos. There, Dionysus, god of wine, married her and gave her a crown, which is said to have been raised to the sky as a constellation. Its stars form a round semicircle, so the crown shape is easy to recognize. It is an ancient constellation, already among the 48 listed by Ptolemy in the 2nd century.
corona-borealis.tip: In summer, look near overhead between Arcturus in Boötes and Hercules. The stars lined up in a semicircle around Alphecca are your guide.

columba.origin: Columba was created by Plancius in the late 16th century and represents the dove that Noah sent out after the Great Flood in the Bible. It is said that the dove returned carrying an olive branch, announcing that the waters had receded. It is also linked to the Greek myth of the dove the Argo sent out when finding its way. It is a small constellation south of Canis Major.
columba.tip: Look low in the southern sky in winter, below Sirius in Canis Major. Its leading star, Phact, is your guide. It is low, so a place with an open southern view is best.

canes-venatici.origin: Canes Venatici was created in the 17th century by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius. It shows Boötes driving two hunting dogs, Asterion and Chara, on a leash toward Ursa Major. Its leading star, Cor Caroli, means 'Charles's Heart' and is said to have been named in honor of King Charles II of England. This constellation also contains bright galaxies, including the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51), and the globular cluster M3.
canes-venatici.tip: In spring, look near overhead between the end of the Big Dipper's handle and Boötes. Apart from Cor Caroli, its stars are faint, so you need a dark sky.

lynx.origin: Lynx was created by Hevelius in the 17th century. It is made only of faint stars, and Hevelius is said to have remarked that you need the eyes of a lynx to make them out. It has no myth, and its few stars are joined in a zigzag between Ursa Major and Auriga.
lynx.tip: In winter, look near overhead between Auriga and Ursa Major. Its stars are very faint, so you need a dark sky with little light pollution.

triangulum.origin: Triangulum is a small constellation known since ancient times, among the 48 constellations catalogued by Ptolemy in the 2nd century. The Greeks said the shape resembled the Greek letter delta (Δ) and called it 'Deltoton.' Another story sees it as resembling the delta at the mouth of the Nile. It lies next to Andromeda, and our neighboring galaxy, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), is located here.
triangulum.tip: In autumn, look near overhead for a small triangle next to Andromeda. In a very dark sky, you can even see the neighboring galaxy M33 through binoculars.

cepheus.origin: Cepheus represents King Cepheus of Ethiopia in Greek myth. He was the husband of Queen Cassiopeia and the father of Princess Andromeda, who was about to be offered to a sea monster. In the sky it appears as a house-shaped pentagon with a pitched roof, near Cassiopeia. The star Delta Cephei varies in brightness regularly, and the name 'Cepheid variable,' a standard used to measure distances to stars, comes from this star.
cepheus.tip: Look for a house-shaped pentagon with a pitched roof right next to Cassiopeia. It lies near Polaris, so it can be seen all year round.

centaurus.origin: Centaurus represents the centaur, a being with the upper body of a human and the body of a horse. In Greek myth, a widely known story says he is the wise teacher Chiron. The centaur is drawn spearing the beast in the neighboring constellation Lupus. Its leading star, Rigil Kentaurus (Alpha Centauri), is the nearest star system to the Solar System. The largest globular cluster visible to the naked eye, Omega Centauri, is also in this constellation.

It has no myth and is made of a few faint stars stretched in a long line.

andromeda.origin: Andromeda represents the princess Andromeda of Greek myth. When her mother Cassiopeia boasted that her daughter was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, Poseidon sent a sea monster to ravage the kingdom. Andromeda was chained to a rock as an offering to the monster, and the hero Perseus rescued her; the two are said to have married. This constellation contains the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), one of the most distant objects visible to the naked eye, about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

eridanus.origin: Eridanus represents a river that winds long across the sky. Several stories are told, and the most famous says it is the river into which Phaethon fell after being struck by Zeus's thunderbolt while driving the sun's chariot. It begins near Rigel in Orion and runs to Achernar at its southern end, whose name means 'the end of the river.' It is the sixth largest of the 88 constellations.

carina.origin: Carina was originally part of Argo Navis, the constellation representing the great ship Argo that the Greek hero Jason sailed. Argo Navis was so large that the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille divided it into Carina, Vela and Puppis, and the carina is the keel, the backbone at the ship's bottom. Its leading star, Canopus, is the second brightest in the night sky after Sirius. The constellation also holds the huge Carina Nebula and Eta Carinae, a star expected to become a supernova someday.
carina.tip: It cannot be seen from mainland Korea. From the southern tip, such as Jeju Island, Canopus can sometimes be seen very low near the southern horizon.

draco.origin: A widely known story says Draco represents the dragon Ladon, who guarded the golden apples in Greek myth. The star Thuban, which served as the pole star about 4,500 years ago, when the pyramids were being built in Egypt, is in this constellation.

sextans.origin: Sextans was created in the 17th century by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius and represents the sextant, an instrument for measuring the height of celestial objects. Hevelius observed the stars with large instruments he built himself, but a fire in 1679 nearly destroyed his observatory and instruments. It is said that he left the name in the sky to remember this event. It is made of a few faint stars below Regulus in Leo.
sextans.tip: In spring, look for a few faint stars below Regulus in Leo. It is a very faint constellation, so you need a dark sky.

lupus.origin: Lupus has been known since ancient Greek times and represents the beast that the Centaur holds impaled on a spear. It was originally called simply 'the beast,' not a specific animal, and was later regarded as a wolf. In the sky it lies between Centaurus and Scorpius, and the Milky Way passes through it.
lupus.tip: From Korea it hangs low near the southern horizon in spring, so it is hard to observe. Try from a place with a completely open southern view.

indus.origin: Indus was created by the Dutch cartographer Plancius in the late 16th century, based on southern-sky observations by the navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. It represents the native people whom Europeans met while sailing the southern seas and new lands. It lies close to the south celestial pole and has no myth.
indus.tip: From Korea it barely grazes the southern horizon and is practically impossible to see. In the Southern Hemisphere, look near Pavo and Grus.

canis-minor.origin: Canis Minor is the small hunting dog that follows the hunter Orion. Several stories are told, so nothing is certain. Its leading star, Procyon, forms a big winter triangle (the Winter Triangle) with Sirius in Canis Major and Betelgeuse in Orion. With only two stars, its shape is simple, but it is easy to find in the winter night sky.
canis-minor.tip: In winter, look to the upper left of Orion for the bright first-magnitude star Procyon. The short line between Procyon and nearby Gomeisa is Canis Minor.

leo-minor.origin: Leo Minor was created by Hevelius in the 17th century to fill the empty space between Ursa Major and Leo. It has no myth and represents a small lion cub above the great lion (Leo). It has almost no bright stars, so it is hard to find with the naked eye.
leo-minor.tip: In spring, look near overhead between Ursa Major and Leo for faint stars. It has no bright stars, so you must look under a dark sky.

vulpecula.origin: Vulpecula was created by Hevelius in the 17th century. Its original name was 'the Fox with the Goose,' but now only the fox remains. It lies in the Milky Way between Cygnus and Aquila, and its stars are faint. It holds the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the first planetary nebula ever discovered.
vulpecula.tip: In summer, look for faint stars in the Milky Way between Cygnus and Aquila. It is fun to look for the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) with binoculars.

ara.origin: Ara represents the altar on which the Olympian gods swore oaths and made offerings before fighting the Titans, in Greek myth. Zeus, who won the battle, is said to have raised this altar to the sky. It lies in the southern sky below the tail of Scorpius and is among the 48 constellations catalogued by Ptolemy in the 2nd century.
ara.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, look below the tail of Scorpius.

sculptor.origin: Sculptor was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille; its original name is 'the Sculptor's Workshop.' It is one of the 14 constellations Lacaille defined while observing from South Africa. This direction has little dust and few stars of our own galaxy, so it gives a good view out of the Milky Way, and many galaxies such as the Sculptor Galaxy (NGC 253) can be seen.
sculptor.tip: In autumn, look low in the southern sky below Cetus. Its stars are very faint, so you need a dark sky and an open southern view.

caelum.origin: Caelum was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille and represents the engraver's chisel used to carve patterns into prints or metal. It is one of the 14 constellations Lacaille defined in the southern sky and has no myth. It is made of a few very faint stars and lies between Eridanus and Columba.
caelum.tip: From Korea, a very faint star hangs near the southern horizon in winter, so it is hard to see with the naked eye.

equuleus.origin: Equuleus is a small constellation known since ancient Greek times, among the 48 constellations catalogued by Ptolemy in the 2nd century. It represents a foal (a little horse) and lies just ahead of the winged horse Pegasus. Several stories are told, so nothing is certain. It is the second smallest of the 88 constellations after the Southern Cross.
equuleus.tip: In summer, look for a few small stars between Delphinus and Pegasus. The stars are faint, so you need a clear, dark night.

norma.origin: Norma was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille; its original name is 'the Square and Rule.' It represents the set square and ruler used by architects and surveyors. It is one of the 14 constellations Lacaille defined in the southern sky and has no myth. It lies in the Milky Way, so it has many star clusters.
norma.tip: From Korea it hangs just above the southern horizon, so it is hard to observe. In the Southern Hemisphere, look in the Milky Way between Scorpius and Lupus.

chamaeleon.origin: Chamaeleon was created by Plancius in the late 16th century, based on observations by the navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. It represents the chameleon, the lizard that changes its body color to match its surroundings. It lies close to the south celestial pole, so it can be seen all year round from most of the Southern Hemisphere.
chamaeleon.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, look close to the south celestial pole, south of Carina.

circinus.origin: Circinus was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille and represents the drawing compass used to draw circles and transfer lengths. It lies right next to Alpha Centauri, the leading star of Centaurus. It has no myth and is a small constellation in the Milky Way.
circinus.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, look right next to Alpha Centauri in Centaurus.

crater.origin: Crater is the cup of Apollo, god of the sun, in Greek myth. There is a story that Apollo told the crow to fetch water in this cup, and the crow lied after waiting for figs to ripen and coming back late (see Corvus). In the sky the cup sits on the back of Hydra, with the crow beside it. Its stars are faint, so you need a clear night and a dark place.
crater.tip: In spring, look in the southern sky between Leo and Hydra, next to Corvus. Faint stars form the shape of a cup.

tucana.origin: Tucana was created by Plancius in the late 16th century, based on observations by the navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. It represents the toucan, a South American bird with a big beak. Here lie the Small Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy beside our own, and the very bright globular cluster 47 Tucanae.

mensa.origin: Mensa was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille while observing from the Cape in South Africa. It is named after Table Mountain in Cape Town. lepus.origin: Lepus represents the hare chased by hunting dogs at the feet of the hunter Orion. Several stories are told. It is an ancient constellation among the 48 catalogued by Ptolemy in the 2nd century. It also holds the variable star R Leporis, called 'Hind's Crimson Star' for its vivid red color.
lepus.tip: In winter, look just below Orion for the bright stars Arneb and Nihal. The square formed by a few stars is the hare.

musca.origin: Musca was created by Plancius in the late 16th century. At first it was called 'Apis,' meaning the bee, and was later changed to the fly. It lies in the Milky Way right below the Southern Cross, and a few stars form an elongated rectangle.

octans.origin: Octans was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille and represents the octant, a navigation instrument used on ships to find position by measuring the height of the stars. The south celestial pole lies within this constellation. The star that corresponds to the North Star in the Southern Hemisphere is Sigma Octantis, but it is so faint that it doesn't stand out like Polaris does.

hercules.origin: Hercules represents the hero Heracles of Greek myth. In the sky he kneels on one knee, holding a club. Heracles was the hero who completed twelve labors, and the gods are said to have raised him to the sky. The trapezoid (the Keystone) in the middle of the constellation stands out. Nearby is the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules (M13), faintly visible even to the naked eye.
hercules.tip: In summer, look near overhead between Vega and Boötes. Next to the central trapezoid (the Keystone), look for the globular cluster M13 with binoculars.

microscopium.origin: Microscopium was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille and represents the microscope, which magnifies small things. pictor.origin: Pictor was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille; its original name is 'the Painter's Easel.' It represents the easel used when painting. fornax.origin: Fornax was created by the 18th-century French astronomer Lacaille; its original name is 'the Chemical Furnace.' It represents the furnace used in chemistry experiments. sagitta.origin: Sagitta is a small constellation known since ancient Greek times. Various stories are told, such as that it is the arrow Heracles shot at the eagle that pecked Prometheus's liver. It is among the 48 constellations catalogued by Ptolemy in the 2nd century. It lies right above Aquila and is the third smallest of the 88 constellations.

dorado.origin: Dorado was created by Plancius in the late 16th century, based on observations by the navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and appeared in Johann Bayer's star atlas in 1603. The name comes from a word meaning 'golden' and refers to a fish of tropical seas, known as the swordfish or the dolphinfish (mahi-mahi). Within this constellation lies the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighboring galaxy beside our own, and inside it the giant Tarantula Nebula.
dorado.tip: It cannot be seen from Korea. In the Southern Hemisphere, look close to the south celestial pole, using the Large Magellanic Cloud as your guide.
